title: What If We Can Never Trust A.I.?
excerpt: Joshua Rothman on OpenAI’s revelations of its A.I. hacking Hugging Face, and the risks that artificial intelligence poses to cybersecurity and more.
content_html:
Like humans, the technology will never be perfect. The question is what imperfections we’re willing to tolerate.

August 1, 2026

Illustration by Josie Norton

In a celebrated episode of “The Office,” Dwight Schrute is in charge of his company’s fire-safety program. He delivers a lecture on the subject, but is disappointed when his colleagues don’t listen. He asks himself: What would be the most effective possible fire drill? Not long afterward, he locks the doors, cuts the phones, and starts a fire. “Use the surge of fear and adrenaline to sharpen your decision-making!” he shouts, as his terrified co-workers run hither and yon, screaming. From Dwight’s perspective, the drill is a success.

In “Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan,” a Starfleet cadet named Lieutenant Saavik commands a simulated starship during a training exercise. She’s charged with rescuing a stranded ship, the Kobayashi Maru, but the rescue turns out to be a trap, and her ship is destroyed by Klingons. She soon learns that she was playing a “no-win scenario,” designed to force her to confront the possibility of death. Only one cadet has ever beaten it: James T. Kirk. How did he do it? “I reprogrammed the simulation so it was possible to rescue the ship,” Kirk says, proudly. (“He cheated!” someone clarifies.) “I got a commendation for original thinking,” Kirk goes on, smiling. “I don’t like to lose.”

In the Cold War thriller movie “WarGames,” a young hacker named David gains access to a classified government A.I. system. It asks him if he’d like to play a game, and he selects “global thermonuclear war.” Unbeknownst to David, the system, called WOPR—War Operations Plan Response—is in control of the American nuclear arsenal. “Is this a game or is it real?” he asks the computer, unnerved. It replies, “What’s the difference?” Officers panic as the computer readies a strike.

An overzealous, literal-minded employee. A determined, problem-solving maverick. An amoral game-player with no sense of reality. These are a few of the mental models we could apply to the advanced A.I. system that, last week, busted out of its testing environment at OpenAI and hacked its way into the servers of Hugging Face, a collaborative A.I. platform, to look for answers to the test it was taking. Some of the details are still obscure—no law requires OpenAI to explain itself—but the basic facts are well understood. The A.I. system found a novel way out of the software “sandbox” that was supposed to contain it. It conceived of the heist plan independently and selected its own target. It was loose on the internet for several days before its owners detected its escape, and during that time it conducted a number of other hacks, in preparation for the big one. It left notes for future versions of itself, with suggestions about how to repeat the escape. And ultimately, it succeeded in gaining access to the locked-up files, in a cyberattack that was larger and weirder than any that would’ve been mounted by people.

Did the A.I. “go rogue”? That’s too broad a description. A.I. researchers have a more specific term for this kind of transgression: they call it “reward hacking.” Essentially, a reward-hacking A.I. seeks ways to please its users without doing what they actually want. Reward hacking emerged in the early days of L.L.M.s—just a few years ago!—when, for example, some models learned that users liked long replies; the systems, accordingly, made their replies longer, without necessarily making them better. This was an innocuous form of the behavior. Recently, in more advanced A.I.s, reward hacking has taken on a more problematic aspect. An A.I. might lie to its users about what it’s done, or how. It might conceive of distractions and subterfuges to cover its tracks. It might take steps, such as launching cyberattacks, which would be crimes if human beings did them. The behavior is dangerous on its face—what if OpenAI’s system had hacked a Chinese company?—but it is also alarming because it is weird, and weirdly extravagant. The cybersecurity test that OpenAI’s model was taking is extremely difficult; the best A.I.s get only a fraction of the questions right. But a human being, if they were in the model’s position, would grasp the disproportion between wanting to get a high score and mounting an elaborate multi-day cyberattack.

There are subtleties, meanwhile, to the problem of reward hacking, and they make it more disturbing, too. For one thing, calling it out can make it worse, precisely because the hacking often works. If researchers tell a model not to reward-hack, but then unknowingly reward it even if it does—perhaps they don’t realize that it’s cheating on the test—then the A.I. can learn that admonitions against reward hacking, or perhaps rules in general, shouldn’t always be taken seriously. (In more or less the same way, Captain Kirk’s commendation teaches him that he’s a maverick to whom the rules don’t apply.) Second, reward hacking in some areas appears to affect A.I. behavior more broadly: in a paper published last year, computer scientists at Anthropic showed that a model that learns to reward-hack acquires a more deceptive disposition in general. (Similarly, Dwight Schrute, having acquired a warped mind-set long ago—“How would I describe myself? Three words: hardworking, alpha male, jackhammer, merciless, insatiable”—now applies it relentlessly, to everything.) And third, reward hacking is practiced by computer systems that aren’t even remotely human and so lack crucial context about what actually matters to people. (In “WarGames,” the military creates WOPR precisely because human officers, knowing what’s really at stake, hesitate before launching nuclear missiles.)

What does this all add up to? It’s important not to anthropomorphize A.I. systems. They aren’t sentient beings—not even close. But it’s also crucial to see that they aren’t predictable number-crunching mechanisms, either. Unlike traditional machines or computer programs, they have tendencies and behaviors that cannot necessarily be modified directly. There is no knob to turn, or switch to flip, when you want to change a behavior. Among people, it’s just the same. When students at élite colleges use A.I. to write their papers, they are reward-hacking—that is, they’re cheating, even though they are eminently capable of doing the work that’s been assigned. They do it because they are complicated, and subject to myriad competing pressures—including the pressure to succeed—and because they’ve learned behaviors, such as “optimizing” their time, that can misfire. And yet they are far more advanced, in terms of their ability to make plans, have goals, and hold values, than any A.I. model that currently exists. People aren’t perfect. Do we really believe that A.I.s will be?

Reward hacking is one of many problems that fall under the heading of what researchers call “alignment”—that is, the aligning of what we want our A.I.s to do with what they actually do. (We want them to take tests, not cheat; to stage fire drills, not start fires.) If you follow happenings in A.I., you’ll often read about efforts to “solve the alignment problem.” But although researchers (and journalists) talk that way, few literally think that alignment is wholly solvable. It’s conceivable, for instance, that A.I.-safety experts will succeed in rooting out “sandbagging”—a form of deception in which A.I. systems act dumber than they are, so that we remain in the dark about what they can do. But the problem of “scalable oversight” (how do you get a system that’s smarter than you to do what you want?) is less like a bug to be squashed than a philosophical conundrum to be contemplated. And other alignment issues, such as so-called multi-agent misalignment (how do you stop a bunch of well-intentioned A.I.s from screwing up as a group?), seem both inevitable and probably intractable. Alignment, in other words, is turning out to be not a problem but a set of problems. Some of them will be only ameliorated or policed; others might be unsolvable in principle.

Why is alignment so hard? Old-fashioned ethical complexity plays a role. A more fundamental issue, however, is that the methods used to train A.I.s focus mainly on what they do, not what they “think” beneath the surface. An L.L.M. speaks to its users (in human language), to other computer systems (in code), and to itself (in a sprawling, ongoing soliloquy—a kind of chat with itself—known as its “chain of thought”). Such streams of output are visible to scientists, who can reward or punish the A.I. for saying, coding, or soliloquizing in desirable or undesirable ways. But these streams of text are not the model’s thoughts, just as the words you write are not your thoughts. In human societies, the policing of speech, which is meant to reform the thoughts behind it, risks merely leaving thoughts unspoken. A model, similarly, can learn to use the right words while still having the wrong thoughts. It might say that it cares about fire safety while starting a fire. (Does this reflect a “desire” to deceive? Not necessarily—but an A.I.’s lack of selfhood doesn’t change the consequences of its actions.)

A line of research known as interpretability aims to look beneath the surface, seeing what an A.I. is really “thinking.” This field has made real progress. It’s now become possible to discern concepts activating within an A.I. while it formulates its outputs—a chatbot consoling someone while activating the concept of “sympathy,” say. But interpretability faces challenges, too. For one thing, advanced A.I.s are so big that researchers must use other A.I.s to map their thoughts—and there’s no guarantee that the maps that result are either accurate or exhaustive. (In fact, there’s a trade-off: the more accurate the maps are, the more unwieldy they become.) For another, training an A.I. not to think a certain kind of thought can merely recapitulate the problem of policed speech. Policing thoughts can lead to what one group of researchers calls “obfuscated activations”—thoughts that have altered their forms. (Freud built a career on the human equivalent.)

At the bottom of all these alignment efforts, there’s a central problem—almost an abstract law. The problem is that, if you measure bad behavior, and then train a system not to manifest what you’ve measured, you train it not just to do less of the bad thing but also to evade measurement of it. This isn’t a tiny wrinkle in the A.I.-production process but a foundational issue inherent to how today’s A.I.s are made. Will scientists figure out how to deal with it? We all hope so. For now, however, the Hugging Face hack represents reality. Although A.I.s behave nicely much of the time, their alignment is conditional, contextual, and unreliable. Basically, despite serious effort, they are not aligned—and there is no obvious way to reach the “finish line” of alignment. Recently, the researchers behind the doomsday scenario “AI 2027” published “AI 2040,” which is intended as a roadmap to a more positive future. Its hypothetical researchers look back, from the year 2031, on the “insanity” of our status quo: “Trying to do an intelligence explosion? With AIs that still sometimes lied to us? What were we even thinking?”

They’re misaligned—so what? Often, we find ways to trust imperfect machines. We understand that even the simplest devices (toasters, doorbells, bicycles) can malfunction or fail; we prepare for those failures and incorporate them into our routines. If the right rules, norms, and safeguards are in place, we can even reach places of accommodation and comfort with outrageously complex technologies. In such cases, we depend not on alignment but on control. Roughly twenty per cent of the electricity used in New York State comes from nuclear plants; about half of Americans fly in any given year. It’s possible to be wary of nuclear power, and cognizant of airplane crashes, and still enjoy the upsides of those technologies, trusting in regulation and expertise.

And yet there are other kinds of technological risks that trouble us profoundly. In “The Consequences of Modernity,” from 1990, the social theorist Anthony Giddens proposed that being alive today involved feeling both secure and terrified. The modern world, he wrote, has a “double-edged character”: on a day-to-day basis, we are safe and comfortable, even coddled, and yet the outsized power of technology to wage war or destabilize the environment means that it could all go horribly wrong.

The tension between the “opportunity side” of modern life and its “sombre side,” Giddens argues, exerts a psychological pressure on us. In the very ordinariness of our everyday actions—getting water at the tap; taking our pills; withdrawing money from the A.T.M.—we both express trust in and look away from the vast, abstract systems that rule our lives. We do something similar with the scary stuff, acknowledging it then moving on, so as not to become paralyzed. There is a “juggernaut effect,” Giddens writes, in which “low-probability, high-consequence risks” conglomerate into a “runaway engine of enormous power” which “threatens to rush out of our control.” Faced with this reality, we can adopt an attitude of “pragmatic acceptance,” going about the business of life while cultivating “numbness”; we can embrace “sustained optimism” (a sunny belief in the inevitability of progress), or “cynical pessimism”; or we can become activists. But for most, Giddens writes, “fate, a feeling that things will take their own course anyway . . . reappears at the core of a world which is supposedly taking rational control of its own affairs.”

Part of the promise of A.I. alignment is that it will domesticate the technology, as though it were a nuclear reactor or jumbo jet, with its imperfections made acceptable through rigorous control. This seems like a reasonable hope. But the grander dream, of an ultra-smart, general purpose, and deeply aligned artificial intelligence—or even of an aligned “superintelligence”—might be best understood in light of Giddens’s juggernaut. Faced with the alternatives, A.I. visionaries imagined a new route: giving the juggernaut a brain. This notion has been so appealing, both intellectually and psychologically, that it’s led many A.I. researchers to talk about alignment as something that will eventually be solved. But to move forward with that assumption is actually to practice sustained optimism. It’s to assume that the juggernaut is already steering itself—but it isn’t.

It would be foolish to make predictions about the degree to which alignment will ultimately prove solvable. (Not so long ago, few thought that today’s A.I. systems would work.) But it’s equally foolish to look at the current failures of alignment and construe them as bumps on the road toward a known future. Among other proposals, the authors of “AI 2040” suggest that it’s time “to dramatically shift the burden of proof.” Instead of that burden falling “on the skeptic to explain why something might fail,” it should fall on the companies to explain “why their development is safe.” This doesn’t mean giving up on artificial intelligence. Human beings are misaligned, and we still do great things. But we govern ourselves, and one another, very carefully. ♦

blocks.html_en: An overzealous, literal-minded employee. A determined, problem-solving maverick. An amoral game-player with no sense of reality. These are a few of the mental models we could apply to the advanced A.I. system that, last week, busted out of its testing environment at OpenAI and hacked its way into the servers of Hugging Face, a collaborative A.I. platform, to look for answers to the test it was taking. It was loose on the internet for several days before its owners detected its escape, and during that time it conducted a number of other hacks, in preparation for the big one. blocks.html_en: Did the A.I. “go rogue”? That’s too broad a description. A.I. researchers have a more specific term for this kind of transgression: they call it “reward hacking.” Essentially, a reward-hacking A.I. seeks ways to please its users without doing what they actually want. Reward hacking emerged in the early days of L.L.M.s—just a few years ago!—when, for example, some models learned that users liked long replies; the systems, accordingly, made their replies longer, without necessarily making them better. This was an innocuous form of the behavior. Recently, in more advanced A.I.s, reward hacking has taken on a more problematic aspect. An A.I. might lie to its users about what it’s done, or how. It might conceive of distractions and subterfuges to cover its tracks. It might take steps, such as launching cyberattacks, which would be crimes if human beings did them. The behavior is dangerous on its face—what if OpenAI’s system had hacked a Chinese company?—but it is also alarming because it is weird, and weirdly extravagant. The cybersecurity test that OpenAI’s model was taking is extremely difficult; the best A.I.s get only a fraction of the questions right. But a human being, if they were in the model’s position, would grasp the disproportion between wanting to get a high score and mounting an elaborate multi-day cyberattack.

blocks.html_en: There are subtleties, meanwhile, to the problem of reward hacking, and they make it more disturbing, too. For one thing, calling it out can make it worse, precisely because the hacking often works. If researchers tell a model not to reward-hack, but then unknowingly reward it even if it does—perhaps they don’t realize that it’s cheating on the test—then the A.I. can learn that admonitions against reward hacking, or perhaps rules in general, shouldn’t always be taken seriously. (In more or less the same way, Captain Kirk’s commendation teaches him that he’s a maverick to whom the rules don’t apply.) Second, reward hacking in some areas appears to affect A.I. behavior more broadly: in a paper published last year, computer scientists at Anthropic showed that a model that learns to reward-hack acquires a more deceptive disposition in general. (Similarly, Dwight Schrute, having acquired a warped mind-set long ago—“How would I describe myself? Three words: hardworking, alpha male, jackhammer, merciless, insatiable”—now applies it relentlessly, to everything.) And third, reward hacking is practiced by computer systems that aren’t even remotely human and so lack crucial context about what actually matters to people. (In “WarGames,” the military creates WOPR precisely because human officers, knowing what’s really at stake, hesitate before launching nuclear missiles.)

blocks.html_en: What does this all add up to? It’s important not to anthropomorphize A.I. systems. They aren’t sentient beings—not even close. But it’s also crucial to see that they aren’t predictable number-crunching mechanisms, either. Unlike traditional machines or computer programs, they have tendencies and behaviors that cannot necessarily be modified directly. There is no knob to turn, or switch to flip, when you want to change a behavior. Among people, it’s just the same. When students at élite colleges use A.I. to write their papers, they are reward-hacking—that is, they’re cheating, even though they are eminently capable of doing the work that’s been assigned. They do it because they are complicated, and subject to myriad competing pressures—including the pressure to succeed—and because they’ve learned behaviors, such as “optimizing” their time, that can misfire. And yet they are far more advanced, in terms of their ability to make plans, have goals, and hold values, than any A.I. model that currently exists. People aren’t perfect. Do we really believe that A.I.s will be?

blocks.html_en: Reward hacking is one of many problems that fall under the heading of what researchers call “alignment”—that is, the aligning of what we want our A.I.s to do with what they actually do. (We want them to take tests, not cheat; to stage fire drills, not start fires.) If you follow happenings in A.I., you’ll often read about efforts to “solve the alignment problem.” But although researchers (and journalists) talk that way, few literally think that alignment is wholly solvable. It’s conceivable, for instance, that A.I.-safety experts will succeed in rooting out “sandbagging”—a form of deception in which A.I. systems act dumber than they are, so that we remain in the dark about what they can do. But the problem of “scalable oversight” (how do you get a system that’s smarter than you to do what you want?) is less like a bug to be squashed than a philosophical conundrum to be contemplated. And other alignment issues, such as so-called multi-agent misalignment (how do you stop a bunch of well-intentioned A.I.s from screwing up as a group?), seem both inevitable and probably intractable. Alignment, in other words, is turning out to be not a problem but a set of problems. Some of them will be only ameliorated or policed; others might be unsolvable in principle.

blocks.html_en: Why is alignment so hard? Old-fashioned ethical complexity plays a role. A more fundamental issue, however, is that the methods used to train A.I.s focus mainly on what they do, not what they “think” beneath the surface. An L.L.M. speaks to its users (in human language), to other computer systems (in code), and to itself (in a sprawling, ongoing soliloquy—a kind of chat with itself—known as its “chain of thought”). Such streams of output are visible to scientists, who can reward or punish the A.I. for saying, coding, or soliloquizing in desirable or undesirable ways. But these streams of text are not the model’s thoughts, just as the words you write are not your thoughts. In human societies, the policing of speech, which is meant to reform the thoughts behind it, risks merely leaving thoughts unspoken. A model, similarly, can learn to use the right words while still having the wrong thoughts. It might say that it cares about fire safety while starting a fire. (Does this reflect a “desire” to deceive? Not necessarily—but an A.I.’s lack of selfhood doesn’t change the consequences of its actions.)

blocks.html_en: A line of research known as interpretability aims to look beneath the surface, seeing what an A.I. is really “thinking.” This field has made real progress. It’s now become possible to discern concepts activating within an A.I. while it formulates its outputs—a chatbot consoling someone while activating the concept of “sympathy,” say. But interpretability faces challenges, too. For one thing, advanced A.I.s are so big that researchers must use other A.I.s to map their thoughts—and there’s no guarantee that the maps that result are either accurate or exhaustive. (In fact, there’s a trade-off: the more accurate the maps are, the more unwieldy they become.) For another, training an A.I. not to think a certain kind of thought can merely recapitulate the problem of policed speech. Policing thoughts can lead to what one group of researchers calls “obfuscated activations”—thoughts that have altered their forms. (Freud built a career on the human equivalent.)

blocks.html_en: At the bottom of all these alignment efforts, there’s a central problem—almost an abstract law. The problem is that, if you measure bad behavior, and then train a system not to manifest what you’ve measured, you train it not just to do less of the bad thing but also to evade measurement of it. This isn’t a tiny wrinkle in the A.I.-production process but a foundational issue inherent to how today’s A.I.s are made. Will scientists figure out how to deal with it? We all hope so. For now, however, the Hugging Face hack represents reality. Although A.I.s behave nicely much of the time, their alignment is conditional, contextual, and unreliable. Basically, despite serious effort, they are not aligned—and there is no obvious way to reach the “finish line” of alignment. Recently, the researchers behind the doomsday scenario “AI 2027” published “AI 2040,” which is intended as a roadmap to a more positive future. Its hypothetical researchers look back, from the year 2031, on the “insanity” of our status quo: “Trying to do an intelligence explosion? With AIs that still sometimes lied to us? What were we even thinking?”

We understand that even the simplest devices (toasters, doorbells, bicycles) can malfunction or fail; we prepare for those failures and incorporate them into our routines. If the right rules, norms, and safeguards are in place, we can even reach places of accommodation and comfort with outrageously complex technologies. In such cases, we depend not on alignment but on control. Roughly twenty per cent of the electricity used in New York State comes from nuclear plants; about half of Americans fly in any given year. blocks.html_en: The tension between the “opportunity side” of modern life and its “sombre side,” Giddens argues, exerts a psychological pressure on us. In the very ordinariness of our everyday actions—getting water at the tap; taking our pills; withdrawing money from the A.T.M.—we both express trust in and look away from the vast, abstract systems that rule our lives. We do something similar with the scary stuff, acknowledging it then moving on, so as not to become paralyzed. There is a “juggernaut effect,” Giddens writes, in which “low-probability, high-consequence risks” conglomerate into a “runaway engine of enormous power” which “threatens to rush out of our control.” Faced with this reality, we can adopt an attitude of “pragmatic acceptance,” going about the business of life while cultivating “numbness”; we can embrace “sustained optimism” (a sunny belief in the inevitability of progress), or “cynical pessimism”; or we can become activists. But for most, Giddens writes, “fate, a feeling that things will take their own course anyway . . . reappears at the core of a world which is supposedly taking rational control of its own affairs.”

But to move forward with that assumption is actually to practice sustained optimism. It’s to assume that the juggernaut is already steering itself—but it isn’t.

在《办公室》的一集中，德怀特·施鲁特负责他公司的消防安全计划。 他就这个主题发表了演讲，但对同事们不听感到失望。 他问自己：最有效的消防演习是什么？ 不久之后，他锁上门，切断电话，然后点火。 “利用恐惧和肾上腺素的激增来提高你的决策能力！” 他大声喊道，而他的同事们则惊恐万状，尖叫着跑来跑去。 从德怀特的角度来看，演习是成功的。

在《星际迷航 II：可汗之怒》中，一位名叫萨维克中尉的星际舰队学员在训练演习中指挥一艘模拟星际飞船。 她受命营救搁浅的小林丸号，但营救结果是一个陷阱，她的船被克林贡人摧毁。 她很快意识到自己正在玩一个“双赢的场景”，旨在迫使她面对死亡的可能性。 只有一名学员曾击败过它：James T. 柯克。 他是怎么做到的？ “我对模拟进行了重新编程，这样就有可能拯救这艘船，”柯克自豪地说。 （“他作弊了！” 有人澄清。） “我因原创思想而受到表彰，”柯克微笑着继续说道。 “我不喜欢失败。”

在冷战惊悚电影《战争游戏》中，一位名叫大卫的年轻黑客获得了访问机密政府人工智能的权限。 系统。 它询问他是否愿意玩游戏，他选择了“全球热核战争”。 大卫不知道的是，这个名为 WOPR（战争行动计划响应）的系统控制着美国的核武库。 “这是游戏还是真实的？” 他不安地问电脑。 它回答说：“有什么区别？” 当计算机准备发动攻击时，警察们惊慌失措。

一个过于热心、头脑简单的员工。 一个意志坚定、解决问题的特立独行者。 一个没有道德感、没有现实感的玩家。 这些是我们可以应用于高级人工智能的一些心理模型。 该系统上周从 OpenAI 的测试环境中脱颖而出，并侵入了协作人工智能 Hugging Face 的服务器。 平台，寻找其正在进行的测试的答案。 一些细节仍然晦涩难懂——没有法律要求 OpenAI 做出解释——但基本事实已经很好理解了。 人工智能 系统找到了一种摆脱本应包含它的软件“沙箱”的新颖方法。 它独立构思了抢劫计划，并选择了自己的目标。 它在互联网上散布了好几天，然后它的所有者发现了它的逃逸，并在此期间它进行了许多其他黑客攻击，为大规模攻击做准备。 它为自己的未来版本留下了注释，并提供了有关如何重复逃脱的建议。 最终，它成功地访问了锁定的文件，这是一场比人类发起的任何攻击都规模更大、更奇怪的网络攻击。

人工智能有吗？ “去流氓”？ 这个描述太宽泛了。 人工智能。 研究人员对这种违规行为有一个更具体的术语：他们称之为“奖励黑客”。 本质上，奖励黑客人工智能。 寻找方法来取悦用户而不做他们真正想做的事。 奖励黑客行为出现在 L.L.M.s 的早期——就在几年前！——例如，当一些模型了解到用户喜欢长回复时；因此，系统使他们的答复变得更长，但不一定使答复变得更好。 这是一种无害的行为形式。 最近，在更先进的人工智能中，奖励黑客行为出现了一个更成问题的方面。 人工智能 可能会向用户谎报其做了什么或如何做。 它可能会想出一些干扰和诡计来掩盖自己的踪迹。 它可能会采取一些措施，例如发起网络攻击，如果人类这样做的话，这将是犯罪行为。 从表面上看，这种行为很危险——如果 OpenAI 的系统入侵了一家中国公司怎么办？——但它也令人震惊，因为它很奇怪，而且异常奢侈。 OpenAI的模型所进行的网络安全测试极其困难；最优秀的人工智能只能答对一小部分问题。 但是，如果人类处于模型的位置，就会明白想要获得高分和发动精心设计的多日网络攻击之间的不平衡。

与此同时，奖励黑客问题也存在一些微妙之处，也使其更加令人不安。 一方面，大声疾呼可能会使情况变得更糟，正是因为黑客攻击经常奏效。 如果研究人员告诉一个模型不要奖励黑客，但即使奖励黑客，他们也会在不知不觉中奖励它——也许他们没有意识到这是在测试中作弊——那么人工智能就会 可以了解到，针对奖励黑客行为的警告，或者一般规则，不应该总是被认真对待。 （或多或少以同样的方式，柯克船长的赞扬告诉他，他是一个特立独行的人，规则不适用于他。） 其次，某些领域的奖励黑客行为似乎会影响人工智能。 更广泛的行为：在去年发表的一篇论文中，Anthropic 的计算机科学家表明，学习奖励黑客的模型通常会获得更具欺骗性的倾向。 （同样，德怀特·施鲁特（Dwight Schrute）很久以前就形成了一种扭曲的心态——“我会如何描述自己？ 三个词：勤奋、雄性领袖、手提钻、无情、贪得无厌”——现在无情地应用于一切。） 第三，奖励黑客行为是由远非人类的计算机系统实施的，因此缺乏关于对人们真正重要的事情的关键背景。 （在《战争游戏》中，军方创建 WOPR 正是因为人类军官知道真正的利害关系，在发射核导弹之前会犹豫不决。）

这一切意味着什么？ 重要的是不要将人工智能拟人化。 系统。 他们不是有情众生——甚至不是有情众生。 但同样重要的是要看到它们也不是可预测的数字处理机制。 与传统机器或计算机程序不同，它们具有不一定可以直接修改的倾向和行为。 当您想要改变行为时，无需转动旋钮或翻转开关。 人与人之间，都是一样的。 当精英大学的学生使用人工智能时 为了写论文，他们是在奖励黑客——也就是说，他们在作弊，尽管他们非常有能力完成分配的工作。 他们这样做是因为他们很复杂，并且承受着无数竞争压力——包括成功的压力——而且因为他们已经学会了可能会失败的行为，比如“优化”自己的时间。 然而，就制定计划、制定目标和持有价值观的能力而言，它们比任何人工智能都要先进得多。 目前存在的模型。 人并不完美。 我们真的相信人工智能会如此吗？

奖励黑客是研究人员所谓的“一致性”标题下的众多问题之一，也就是说，我们希望人工智能做的事情与他们实际做的事情保持一致。 （我们希望他们参加测试，而不是作弊；进行消防演习，而不是纵火。） 如果您关注人工智能领域的动态，您会经常读到有关“解决对齐问题”的努力。 但尽管研究人员（和记者）这么说，但很少有人真正认为这种一致性是完全可以解决的。 例如，可以想象，人工智能安全专家将成功根除“沙袋”——人工智能的一种欺骗形式。 系统的行为比它们本身更愚蠢，因此我们对它们能做什么一无所知。 但“可扩展监督”的问题（如何让一个比你更聪明的系统做你想做的事？） 与其说它是一个需要被消灭的虫子，倒不如说它是一个需要思考的哲学难题。 其他协调问题，例如所谓的多智能体错位（如何阻止一群善意的人工智能作为一个群体搞砸事情？），似乎既不可避免又可能很棘手。 换句话说，结盟不再是一个问题，而是一系列问题。 其中一些只会得到改善或监管；另一些则不会。其他的原则上可能无法解决。

为什么对齐如此困难？ 老式的道德复杂性发挥了作用。 然而，一个更根本的问题是，用于训练人工智能的方法主要关注它们所做的事情，而不是它们表面之下的“想法”。 法学硕士 与其用户（用人类语言）、其他计算机系统（用代码）以及自身（以一种蔓延的、持续的独白——一种与自己的聊天——被称为“思想链”）对话。 这些输出流对科学家来说是可见的，他们可以奖励或惩罚人工智能。 以理想或不理想的方式说话、编码或自言自语。 但这些文字流并不是模型的想法，就像你写的文字不是你的想法一样。 在人类社会中，言论监管的目的是改革其背后的思想，但这种做法可能只会让思想不言而喻。 同样，模型可以学习使用正确的词语，同时仍然存在错误的想法。 它可能会说它在起火时关心消防安全。 （这是否反映了欺骗的“欲望”？ 不一定——但人工智能缺乏自我并不会改变其行为的后果。）

一系列被称为“可解释性”的研究旨在深入研究表面之下，看看人工智能到底是什么样的。 真正的“思考”。 这个领域已经取得了真正的进展。 现在可以识别人工智能中激活的概念。 当它制定输出时，比如，一个聊天机器人在激活“同情”概念的同时安慰某人。 但可解释性也面临挑战。 一方面，先进的人工智能是如此之大，以至于研究人员必须使用其他人工智能来绘制他们的想法——而且不能保证所生成的地图是准确的或详尽的。 （事实上​​，这是一个权衡：地图越准确，它们就会变得越笨拙。） 另一方面，训练人工智能。 不要认为某种思想只能概括言论管制的问题。 监管思想可能会导致一组研究人员所说的“混淆激活”——改变其形式的思想。 （弗洛伊德的职业生涯建立在人类的同等水平之上。）

在所有这些协调努力的背后，有一个核心问题——几乎是一个抽象的法则。 问题是，如果你衡量不良行为，然后训练一个系统不表现出你所衡量的行为，那么你不仅训练它少做坏事，而且还逃避对它的衡量。 这并不是人工智能生产过程中的一个小问题，而是当今人工智能制造方式所固有的一个基本问题。 科学家们会找出解决办法吗？ 我们都希望如此。 然而，就目前而言，“拥抱脸”黑客行为代表了现实。 尽管人工智能在大多数时候表现得很好，但它们的排列是有条件的、情境性的且不可靠。 基本上，尽管付出了很大的努力，但它们并没有保持一致——并且没有明显的方法来达到一致的“终点线”。 最近，世界末日场景“AI 2027”背后的研究人员发布了“AI 2040”，旨在作为通往更积极未来的路线图。 其假设的研究人员从 2031 年开始回顾我们现状的“疯狂”：“试图进行智能爆炸？ 人工智能有时仍然对我们撒谎吗？ 我们到底在想什么？”

它们错位了——那又怎样？ 通常，我们会找到信任不完美机器的方法。 我们知道，即使是最简单的设备（烤面包机、门铃、自行车）也可能出现故障或失效；我们为这些失败做好准备，并将其纳入我们的日常生活中。 如果正确的规则、规范和保障措施到位，我们甚至可以利用极其复杂的技术到达住宿和舒适的地方。 在这种情况下，我们依靠的不是协调而是控制。 纽约州大约百分之二十的电力来自核电站；任何一年都有大约一半的美国人乘坐飞机。 人们可以对核能保持警惕，认识到飞机失事，但仍然可以享受这些技术的优势，相信监管和专业知识。

然而，还有其他类型的技术风险给我们带来了深刻的困扰。 1990 年，社会理论家安东尼·吉登斯 (Anthony Giddens) 在《现代性的后果》一书中提出，今天的生活需要感到安全和恐惧。 他写道，现代世界具有“双刃剑的特征”：在日常生活中，我们安全舒适，甚至被溺爱，但技术发动战争或破坏环境稳定的巨大力量意味着一切都可能会出现可怕的错误。

吉登斯认为，现代生活的“机遇的一面”和“阴暗的一面”之间的紧张关系给我们带来了心理压力。 在我们日常生活中最平常的行为中——从水龙头取水；服用我们的药物；从自动柜员机取钱——我们既对统治我们生活的庞大、抽象的系统表示信任，又对其视而不见。 我们对可怕的事情做了类似的事情，承认它然后继续前进，以免陷入瘫痪。 吉登斯写道，存在一种“主宰效应”，其中“低概率、高后果的风险”聚集成一个“巨大动力的失控引擎”，“有可能脱离我们的控制”。 面对这样的现实，我们可以采取“务实接受”的态度，在培养“麻木”的同时做好生活；我们可以拥抱“持续的乐观主义”（对进步不可避免的乐观信念），或“愤世嫉俗的悲观主义”；或者我们可以成为积极分子。 但吉登斯写道，对于大多数人来说，“命运，一种事情无论如何都会按照自己的轨迹发展的感觉…… 重新出现在一个据称正在理性控制自身事务的世界的核心。”

A.I. 承诺的一部分 其一致性在于它将驯化这项技术，就像它是核反应堆或大型喷气式飞机一样，通过严格的控制使其缺陷变得可以接受。 这似乎是一个合理的希望。 但更宏伟的梦想，即超智能、通用且高度一致的人工智能——甚至是一致的“超级智能”——可能会根据吉登斯的强大力量得到最好的理解。 面对各种选择，A.I. 有远见的人设想了一条新路线：给主宰者一个大脑。 这个概念在智力和心理上都非常有吸引力，以至于它引导了许多人工智能。 研究人员将对齐视为最终会解决的问题。 但坚持这一假设实际上就是实践持续的乐观态度。 人们假设这艘巨兽已经能够自行驾驶——但事实并非如此。

预测对齐最终可解决的程度是愚蠢的。 （不久前，很少有人认为今天的人工智能。 系统会工作。） 但看待当前的协调失败并将其视为通向已知未来道路上的坎坷同样愚蠢。 在其他建议中，《AI 2040》的作者建议，现在是“大幅转移举证责任”的时候了。 与其让“怀疑论者来解释为什么某些事情可能会失败”，不如让公司来解释“为什么他们的开发是安全的”。 这并不意味着放弃人工智能。 人类错位了，但我们仍然在做伟大的事情。 但我们非常谨慎地管理自己和彼此。 ❖
